entries.clue: Efforts made to have tin glaze initially added to artworks (9)

indicatorNotes.made to have: Something made to have another thing is made to hold it, so the shorter run of letters goes inside the longer rather than beside it.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially points at a word as it starts out, so only the opening letter of the word it follows is taken.

blocks.note: efforts that cost you something are pains, as in taking pains over a job
the metal stands as its own three letters
the letter the word starts with

annotation.surface: A craftsman's efforts with tin and a first coat of glaze, all going into some artworks.
annotation.walkthrough: Glaze sits in the surface as something a potter brushes on and hands over a single letter. The newcomers land between the last two letters of the efforts, which is why the join is so hard to see.
annotation.definitionFit: Artworks covers anything made as art, and pictures in paint are its most familiar kind, so the wider word names them by their class.

entries.clue: Leading role Spooner might have toasted? (3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a thing and 'toasted' is what is done to it; the question mark flags that the setter is naming the pastry by its treatment rather than by a synonym.

indicatorNotes.Spooner might have: Spooner was the Oxford don remembered for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so a clue in his name asks you to make that swap yourself.

blocks.note: the leading role in a play is the top part, and trading the opening sounds of those two words spells something else entirely

annotation.surface: Spooner raising a glass to whoever landed the starring role.
annotation.walkthrough: The reverend's swap works on sounds, so you have to say the two words before you can hear the other pair inside them. 'Toasted' changes trade as well: a glass in the surface, a toaster in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A Pop-Tart is a filled pastry sold to be dropped in a toaster, so 'toasted' names it by the one thing everybody does with it.

entries.clue: Japanese art has elements of childlike banality (7)

indicatorNotes.elements of: Elements of a phrase are a part taken out of it, so the letters wanted are sitting unbroken inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the seven letters run unbroken from four letters into the first word across the gap and into the second

annotation.surface: A Japanese art form accused of drawing on a child's plainness of mind.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden runs rarely sit this openly across a word break, and 'like' reads as ordinary English until you stop seeing the gap. Ikebana is the Japanese discipline of arranging cut flowers to strict rules.
annotation.definitionFit: Ikebana is the formal Japanese art of flower arranging, so the definition names it by its country and its kind.

entries.clue: He had agents swarming around pub? (3,4,4)

indicatorNotes.swarming around: Things swarming around are not where they were put, and letters that will not stay put have to be written in some other order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: A spymaster whose agents are buzzing about outside a pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'He had agents' reads as the opening of a spy story and is nothing but eleven letters of fodder. The question mark is the setter admitting that one particular pub is standing in for pubs in general.
annotation.definitionFit: The Nag's Head is a stock name on British pub signs, the Peckham local in Only Fools and Horses being the famous one, so 'pub' defines it by example.

entries.clue: Scotch producer reports there’s no bouquet developing? (7)

indicatorNotes.Scotch producer reports: A producer of Scotch is a Scot, and words reported from his mouth come out in Scots rather than in standard English.

blocks.note: na is the Scots form of no, the way it is said and written north of the border
the bouquet of a wine or a whisky is its scent

annotation.surface: A distiller reporting that the spirit in the cask is throwing no nose at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reports' invites you to listen for a homophone and is only telling you whose accent to borrow. Bouquet is the taster's word for a smell, which is why a drinks trade sits so comfortably in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Something nascent has only just come into being and is still forming, which is what calling a thing developing says about it.

entries.clue: Arranged to have piano inside played (7)

indicatorNotes.inside: What goes inside something sits within its letters rather than in front of or behind them.

blocks.note: a matter that has been arranged has been sorted
p is the mark written in a score for piano, the instruction to play softly

annotation.surface: An arrangement made so that a piano could be played in the house.
annotation.walkthrough: The piano is the one written as p in sheet music, not the furniture, which is why an instrument gives up a single letter. Sport as a verb means to play or frolic, an old sense that crosswords have kept alive.
annotation.definitionFit: To sport is to play or amuse oneself, the sense in 'sporting with', so the past tense of one verb answers for the past tense of the other.

entries.clue: Love to get two degrees? Yes we can, he said (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is not a synonym but a quotation with its speaker attached: the answer is the man who said the words.

blocks.note: love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, and nothing is written as the round letter
a BA and an MA, the bachelor's and the master's, run together in that order

annotation.surface: An encouraging reply to the idea of taking two university degrees for the love of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yes we can' was the chant of the 2008 presidential campaign, so the definition names a man by his slogan and leaves 'he said' to do the pointing. Love for nothing comes from the tennis court.
annotation.definitionFit: Barack Obama made 'Yes we can' the refrain of his 2008 campaign, chanted back at him from every rally, so the words with 'he said' identify the speaker.

entries.clue: Travelling while ill (3)

blocks.note: departed and on the way, the sense used of a runner the instant a race starts
under the weather, the sense in which a person is a bit out of sorts or milk has gone bad

annotation.surface: Someone away on a journey and unwell at the same time.
annotation.walkthrough: Three letters carry two quite separate senses, and 'while' is the only join in the clue — it contributes nothing of its own. The same little word also describes milk that has gone bad.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who is off has left and is on their way, and someone feeling off is unwell: the one word covers the journey and the malady.

entries.clue: Jump in as there’s plenty that does this (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of matching it word for word: 'this' is the verb itself, and what plenty does is the thing being defined.

indicatorNotes.in: Something told to go in lands within the word that follows rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: the two letters of the little word itself, parting to take the jump
a jump is a bound, the word for a single springing leap

annotation.surface: An invitation to join in because there is more than enough to go round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jump in' looks like one phrase and is two instructions: the jump is a word to find, the 'in' says where to put it. The definition is the whole tail of the clue, pointing at itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Where something abounds there is plenty of it, the verb saying of a thing that it exists in quantity.

entries.clue: She performs in a style not approved by the Guardian? (7)

blocks.note: a woman who acts for a living, on a stage or in front of a camera

blocks.clueFragment: in a style not approved by the Guardian?
blocks.note: read as a manner of performing the paper dislikes, and meant as its style guide, which tells its journalists to call women actors like everyone else

annotation.surface: A performer whose manner on stage is not to the paper's taste.
annotation.walkthrough: The Guardian's style guide is the book its writers follow on spelling and usage, and it rules this particular word out of the paper. Nothing is shuffled or hidden — the joke is that the setter's own employer bans the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The word names a woman who performs, and the Guardian's style guide tells its writers to use 'actor' for women too — the ban the clue points at.

entries.clue: Bother first lady after exercise (5)

indicatorNotes.after: After is a statement of order, and what comes after a thing is written behind it.

blocks.note: PE is physical education, the exercise lesson on a school timetable
Eve is the first woman in Genesis, the original first lady

annotation.surface: A warning not to trouble the President's wife once her workout is over.
annotation.walkthrough: The First Lady of the surface lives in the White House; the one the clue wants comes from the Book of Genesis. 'Bother' is a verb here, not a noun, which is why the answer is a verb too.
annotation.definitionFit: To peeve someone is to irritate them in a small way, which is bothering them in the everyday sense.

entries.clue: Betray apparent leader seen on the street (4,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description of where the answer is found rather than a noun: what you see on the street is the thing itself.

blocks.note: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them to the police
a front is the visible figure put up to head a business, the apparent leader rather than the real one

annotation.surface: An informer giving up the man who only appeared to be in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shop' for betray is the language of the police cell — to shop a man is to name him to the law. The two halves are simply written one after the other, with no instruction in the clue at all.
annotation.definitionFit: A shopfront is the glazed face a shop turns towards the pavement, so it is precisely what is seen on the street.

entries.clue: Pangram will regularly display this range (3)

indicatorNotes.will regularly display: What is shown regularly is shown at even intervals, so the letters come out at every second step instead of all together.

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters in turn: p-A-n-G-r-A-m

annotation.surface: A pangram showing off the full range of the alphabet.
annotation.walkthrough: A pangram is a sentence using every letter, which is the range the surface means. The range the clue means is an Aga, the cast-iron cooker that sits in an English kitchen and is never turned off.
annotation.definitionFit: An Aga is a heavy cast-iron cooker, a brand so common in British kitchens that its name stands for the range itself.

entries.clue: A man like Trump that devastates the environment (5,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a substance and the definition is what it does, a verb phrase hanging off 'A man' in the surface; the setter defines the chemical by its effect.

blocks.note: the article taken as it stands
a gent is a man, the everyday short form of gentleman
the colour cartoonists give the US president, from his much-mocked tan

annotation.surface: A tanned businessman being blamed for wrecking the planet.
annotation.walkthrough: Agent Orange was the defoliant the Americans sprayed over Vietnam, named for the orange stripe painted round its drums — so the colour is in the answer for a quite different reason than in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Agent Orange, the dioxin-laced defoliant sprayed over Vietnam, stripped the forests and poisoned the ground for decades, which is devastation of the environment.

entries.clue: Tease prince worried when rip expanded (4,2,5)

indicatorNotes.worried: To worry a thing is to shake it about the way a dog worries a rag, and letters shaken about come out in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: A prince growing anxious as the tear in his clothes gets bigger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rip' is a tear in the surface and three letters cut on a gravestone in the clue, and expanding an abbreviation means writing it out in full. Nothing in the answer is torn.
annotation.definitionFit: RIP is carved on headstones for rest in peace, so expanding those three letters gives the words themselves.

entries.clue: Managed to rest after tension in crossing (7)

indicatorNotes.after: After fixes the order of the pieces: whatever comes after the tension is written behind it.

blocks.note: T is the physicist's symbol for tension, the letter labelling a rope in a force diagram
someone who managed a business ran it
to rest your legs is to sit

annotation.surface: Someone who coped and then sat down once the stress had passed.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue's order is not the answer's: the tension is named last in the wordplay and stands first in the grid. 'Rest' offers the remainder and delivers the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A transit is a crossing from one side to the other, the passage a ship makes or a planet makes across the face of the sun.

entries.clue: Stops son joining uncaring god worshippers (7)

indicatorNotes.joining: Someone joining a group goes in among them, so the letter takes its place inside the word rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: deists believe in a creator who made the world and has taken no interest in it since
S is the standard short form of son, as written on a family tree

annotation.surface: A son signing up with a congregation that worships an indifferent god.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Uncaring' is not a judgement on the worshippers but part of what their belief says: the god of deism leaves the world alone. To desist is to stop of your own accord, which is why the definition is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To desist is to leave off doing something, matching 'stops' in the sense of ceasing rather than of blocking.

entries.clue: Small change as regularly spotted on the beat (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half describes the answer rather than translating it: the ones regularly spotted on the beat are police officers.

blocks.note: the copper coins in your pocket, the pennies and twopences of loose change
British slang for police officers, the beat being the fixed round a constable walks

annotation.surface: Loose coins turning up again and again on a constable's round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like the instruction to take every other letter and means nothing more here than often. Both halves of the clue settle on the same street, which is what lets the surface read as one sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Copper coins are the pennies of small change, and 'copper' has been British slang for a police officer since the 1840s, from cop, to catch.

entries.clue: Direct passage is sound (7)

blocks.note: a way running straight through from one side to the other, whether for water, for shipping or for a broadcast
in geography a sound is a narrow stretch of water joining two larger ones, as in Plymouth Sound

annotation.surface: Advice that a route straight through is the sensible one to take.
annotation.walkthrough: Direct, passage and sound each name the answer on their own, so the clue is really three definitions stacked in one short sentence. 'Sound' reads as sensible and means a strait.
annotation.definitionFit: A channel is a passage running straight from one side to the other, most famously the water between England and France; a sound is the same thing under another name.

entries.clue: Gradually develop page design (4,3)

blocks.note: p is the standard short form of page, as in 'see p 34'
the layout of a page is its design, the placing of type and pictures on it

annotation.surface: An instruction to work a page design up slowly.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration hides the join: the answer breaks after four letters and the wordplay breaks after one. Events that play out unfold step by step towards their end, which is the sense the definition wants.
annotation.definitionFit: When events play out they unfold at their own pace until they are finished, which is what gradually developing describes.

entries.clue: Knock out part of flood defence (7)

blocks.note: to club a man senseless, originally with a sock or bag of sand, which leaves no mark on him
one of the filled sacks stacked in a wall across a doorway when the river comes up

annotation.surface: An order to demolish a section of the river barrier.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an instruction to knock a hole in something; the clue is two senses of one object. Sacks of sand stacked at a door are the standard British defence against a rising river, and the same bag makes an improvised cosh.
annotation.definitionFit: A sandbag is a sack of sand stacked against rising water, and to sandbag someone is to knock them out with one — one object, noun and verb.

entries.clue: Servant retains half of treats for one overseeing service (6,1)

indicatorNotes.retains: What a thing retains it keeps inside itself, so the shorter run of letters ends up within the longer word.
indicatorNotes.half of: Half of a six-letter word is three letters, and with nothing said about which half, it is the first three.

blocks.note: a maid is a household servant
the first half of that six-letter word, taken from its front

annotation.surface: A servant holding back some of the treats meant for the man in charge of the dining room.
annotation.walkthrough: The service being overseen is a restaurant's, not a church's or a car's. Maître d' is short for maître d'hôtel, the head waiter who runs the front of house and seats the diners.
annotation.definitionFit: The maître d' runs the floor of a restaurant, greeting guests and directing the waiters, so he is the one overseeing service.

entries.clue: Here in Rome, complain about hairstyle (7)

indicatorNotes.about: To be about something is to be round it, so one word wraps itself around the other.

blocks.note: to complain is to moan
hic is the Latin for here, and 'in Rome' is the setter asking for the Latin word

annotation.surface: A grumble heard in Rome about somebody's haircut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Rome' is the standard way of asking for Latin, and hic — the word on tombstones in hic jacet, here lies — is its 'here'. The crest of hair takes its name from the Mohican people, though the style belongs to the Mohawk.
annotation.definitionFit: A mohican is the haircut with the sides shaved and a stiff crest left standing down the middle, named after the Native American people.

entries.clue: Harsh sounding political line carried by newspaper (7)

indicatorNotes.carried by: What is carried by something is held inside it, so those letters sit within the word that carries them.

blocks.note: a rag is a newspaper, usually one the speaker thinks little of
spin is the favourable line a party puts on the facts, the trade of the spin doctor

annotation.surface: A party's severe-sounding message being carried in a downmarket paper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sounding' belongs to the definition and not to any homophone — the word describes a voice that grates on the ear. A rag is a newspaper, and spin is what a press officer puts on the news it prints.
annotation.definitionFit: A rasping voice is rough and grating, which is harsh sounding in the plainest sense of both words.

entries.clue: Kill little dog upset when redecorating (5,2)

indicatorNotes.upset: In a down clue something upset has been turned on its head, so its letters are read back up the grid.

blocks.note: to do someone in is to kill them, and the four letters run straight on
a pug is a small flat-faced dog, here written upwards

annotation.surface: A small dog so upset by the decorating that somebody threatens to kill it.
annotation.walkthrough: The break in the answer falls one letter into the dog, so the pieces never line up with the spaces. 'Upset' works as it does because the entry runs down the grid, where turning a word round means reading it upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Doing up a house means redecorating and refurbishing it, the phrase every estate agent uses for a place that needs work.

entries.clue: Titanic orchestra perhaps, and what they didn’t do (7,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a clause about the musicians rather than a synonym: the answer is the thing they never did.

blocks.note: an orchestra at sea is a group of players aboard a vessel, and with the article in front those words respace, letter for letter, into something else

annotation.surface: The Titanic's musicians, playing on as the water rose.
annotation.walkthrough: Written out, the wordplay says a band on ship, and the same eleven letters respace into the order shouted at a wreck. The Titanic's musicians famously played on rather than taking to the boats.
annotation.definitionFit: Abandon ship is the order to leave a sinking vessel, and the Titanic's band played on instead of obeying it, so the definition names the thing they never did.

entries.clue: Runner should keep improving from the start (3)

indicatorNotes.from the start: Taking words from the start means taking them at their opening letters and going no further into them.

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the three words in turn

annotation.surface: A sprinter told to get better and keep getting better.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runner' reads as an athlete and names a thing that slides instead — the same word covers the blades under a sledge. The rest of the clue is ordinary coaching talk until you read only its initials.
annotation.definitionFit: A ski is a runner: a long smooth strip that carries weight over snow, the sense the word has in a sledge's runners.

entries.clue: No hope revolutionary writer is preferring old stuff? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The word is a fear of the new rather than a love of the old; the question mark admits the setter is defining it by the consequence.

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: A revolutionary overturns the established order, and the order overturned here is the order of the letters.

blocks.note: six letters shuffled into a new order
a Bic is the cheap ballpoint everybody loses, a writer in the pen sense rather than the author

annotation.surface: A hopeless revolutionary author with a taste for the past.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer' wants to be an author and is a biro. 'Revolutionary' reads as a political type in the surface and is the instruction to overturn the two words in front of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone neophobic shrinks from anything new, and shrinking from the new leaves the old, which is what the question mark is apologising for.

entries.clue: Spring finishes off with Tokyo trip (3)

indicatorNotes.finishes off: The finish of a word is the letter it ends on, and finishing off several words takes that last letter from each of them.

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the three words in turn

annotation.surface: The season ending with a journey out to Japan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring' is the season in the surface and a verb in the definition, which is the whole of the misdirection. A hop is also a single leg of a long flight, so the answer could almost belong to the trip.
annotation.definitionFit: To hop is to spring lightly off the ground, the same small jump that the verb spring describes.

entries.clue: Threatening to exclude men passing challenge with ease (5)

indicatorNotes.exclude: To exclude something is to shut it out, so those letters are dropped from the word that held them.

blocks.note: something threatening is menacing
the three letters shut out, taken from the front of that word

annotation.surface: A threat to keep men out of something they were sailing through.
annotation.walkthrough: The men are excluded from the front of a word, not from the club the surface imagines. To ace a test began as American slang and is now ordinary English on both sides of the Atlantic.
annotation.definitionFit: Acing an exam or an interview is getting through it with room to spare, from the ace that beats every other card.

entries.clue: Moderation of rent increase (3-2)

blocks.note: to let a flat is to rent it out, the British landlord's word for it
to up a price is to increase it

annotation.surface: A landlord going easy on the size of a rent rise.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about housing costs, which is what hides the join between its two words. Both halves keep their everyday meanings, so there is no instruction anywhere in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A let-up is an easing off — of rain, of pressure, of effort — so moderation in the sense of slackening, not of restraint.

entries.clue: Liberal agreed GNP reveals societal disparity (6,3)

indicatorNotes.Liberal: Liberal here means free and loose rather than strict, and letters handled loosely need not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A Liberal politician accepting that the national output figures expose an inequality.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' reads as the party, and the capital letter is doing its usual cover job at the start of a sentence. GNP is gross national product, the measure of everything a country produces in a year.
annotation.definitionFit: The gender gap is the measured difference between women and men in pay, health or voting, which is a disparity running across society.
